Posted August 13, 2002

Analysis by Richard Cowan

First, let me make very clear that although I have misgivings about some of its aspects -- I support Question 9, the Nevada initiative that would attempt to legalize marijuana, and if I lived in the state, I would vote for it.

It should also go without saying that NORML supports Question 9, which it does.

That I have to begin with such a statement is a part of the story that I will discuss below.

" Regulation " versus the " L " word.

Let me also make very clear that I am in favor of the " legalization " of cannabis.
See

But there are those that think that such a statement really should " go without saying. "

Polls generally indicate that the much of the public has been conditioned to react negatively to the word " legalize. " After all, anything that is " legal " must therefore be both harmless for everyone and at least morally neutral, just like alcohol, guns, over-the-counter medications, etc.??

Recently, an editorial in the Wall Street Journal on the proposed changes to UK cannabis laws referred pejoratively to " U.S. legalizers " and warned, " For the U.S., the lesson would appear to be to beware legalizers bearing British gifts. "
See

NORML actually has a picture of a prohibitionist group with a sign saying, " Death to pushers and legalizers. " Hate-mongering works.

Consequently, some anti-prohibitionists argue that we should avoid the " L " word in favor of " regulation " or almost anything else. That argument becomes more urgent in the political context of an initiative, such as that underway in Nevada.

I respectfully disagree.

I think we should say what we mean, because the destruction of meaning is a big part of the war on freedom.

As I wrote in 1999, " I think that the most important feature of 1984 is " Newspeak " and " Doublethink. " Orwell even wrote an Appendix to 1984, " The Principles of Newspeak. "

As Orwell explained, the purpose of Newspeak was not just to provide a medium of expression, but to make " heretical thought .literally unthinkable. "

" To give a single example. The word free still existed in Newspeak, but it could only be used in such statements as This dog is free of lice or This field is free of weeds. It could not be used in the old sense of politically free or intellectually free, since political and intellectual freedom no longer existed even as concepts, and were therefore of necessity nameless. "
See

Of course, all of this is easy for me to say. I sit here in my ivory tower writing about abstractions, while those in the trenches are trying to stop people from getting arrested. However, as we shall see, all of this has real world significance, if Nevada is the real world.

The best/worst argument.

The Nevada initiative effort is being managed by a group called

As its name implies, the principle argument being used by Question 9's sponsors is that marijuana prohibition is not a responsible use of law enforcement resources. That is perfectly true, plus it has the advantage of being the argument that gets the highest positive support in polls.

That is why I call this line the " best/worst " argument for ending cannabis prohibition. It is the best in that it appeals to many people who might otherwise oppose any reforms. With law enforcement in crisis in the UK, Canada, and DEAland, especially after 9/11, it is a particularly compelling argument.
See

However, it is also the worst argument because it is appalling to think that freedom can be justified best as a byproduct of police efficiency. People, especially in the context of the western tradition of individual freedom, should have the right to use a plant so long as they are not harming others.

Cannabis should be legalized because it should never have been made illegal in the first place.
See

Cannabis should be legalized because cannabis prohibition is a counterproductive fraud.
See

Cannabis should be legalized because, if an argument is to be couched in terms of the role of the police, arbitrary police power is a threat to everyone's freedom.
See
Saving the Law from Law Enforcement. Ending the Police State Fraud. Analysis by Richard Cowan

In the present context, such arguments may not get the best immediate polling results, but they appeal to fundamental American values. As Martin Luther King said of the civil rights movement, we will win because we are not asking America or Britain or Canada to change their fundamental principles, but to live up to them.

The Constitution of the United States does not begin with the statement, " We the people of the United States, in order to create more responsible law enforcement. "

No, thank you.

However, even at the " most pragmatic " level, trying to spin the public perception of the issue does not work very well.
See
We Are Winning! Almost One Third In DEAland Now Support " Legalization " of Marijuana 40% In The West. In the Face of the Massive Prohibitionist Propaganda Campaign and Spin Control in Polling.
and
We Are Still Winning! Almost A Third of DEAland " Agree that Marijuana Should Be Legalized. " Okay, But More Than That Voted for Legalization Plus in Alaska.

First, whatever we call an initiative, whatever its subject matter, the prohibitionists will say that it " legalizes " marijuana. Indeed, even the most restrictive medical marijuana initiatives were portrayed as " legalizing " marijuana as a part of a plot to legalize all drugs for small children. I can almost always predict what the prohibitionist will say, meaning which lie they will tell.

And when an initiative is proposed that, according to the NRLE home page, would " Require the state government to implement a system whereby adults could obtain marijuana through a legally regulated market, rather than from the criminal market ", I say bravo, but that is " legalization. "

And it did not take the Nevada Conference of Police and Sheriffs (NCOPS) very long to figure that out, after it was announced that they had endorsed the initiative.

Last weekproduced one of the weirdest events that I can recall in the weird history of the cannabis reform movement. First, it was announced that Nevada Conference of Police and Sheriffs board had unanimously endorsed Question 9, then it was announced that they had not. It was all a mistake. Oops!

The Las Vegas Review-Journal reported that the NCOPS board members now claim " that an official vote never took place and that they believed any discussions on the issue concerned medical use of marijuana, not legalization. "

One member is quoted as saying, " I thought it was something we were going to place on the agenda for a future vote. I was not aware we were looking to take a vote. This is important enough to discuss the pros and cons. ... I believed I was just chatting. "

My favorite statement came from a " former vice officer, " who said, " It's sure to be pretty much a no-brainer, " he said. " They'll say sorry we've made a mistake, and we're not supporting it. "

A no-brainer indeed!

Well, I love watching the narks fight among themselves, and this certainly might undermine their credibility, but unless that was the real objective, it was not exactly a famous victory.

How could this happen? Well, here are some clues.

Even before this particular fiasco, it had become clear that the media were not fooled by spin that Question 9 was not about legalization. Friendly and competent reporters and there are some want to report it straight, and the prohibitionist media will always sensationalize it.

Spin City is a sitcom, not a strategy.

Now the sponsors of Question 9 are scrambling to find someone to blame. And who do they blame? Why NORML, of course.

How is this? Well, the July 30th New York Times ran an article under the header: " Nevadans Weigh Proposal to Make Marijuana Legal " and in the article they quoted Keith Stroup, NORML's founder and Executive Director as saying " This is a landmark initiative that seeks more than what any state has accomplished so far. "

" Mr. Stroup cautioned, however, that the Nevada effort might be too ambitious to succeed.

While states have reduced penalties for some marijuana offenses without interference from the federal government, he said any measure that put a state in the drug business would violate federal law and draw a challenge from the Justice Department.

In general, when state law conflicts with federal law, the federal law takes precedence, giving federal prosecutors the discretion to pursue a case or not. A state-regulated drug operation, Mr. Stroup said, would be too much for the federal government to ignore.

" It is highly unlikely the federal government would allow a state to create a legal market for the sale of drugs in which the state licenses the sale or sets up stores to sell it, " he said.

" But what it would do is place enormous pressure on Congress to take a rational look at the nation's drug laws.

" As we begin to get more and more states considering legalization, it will be impossible for Congress to stand in their way. "

Why would anyone argue that such a statement undermines the initiative drive?

Well, it turns out that NRLE is really just a front for the Marijuana Policy Project, a DC based group, funded by Ohio billionaire Peter Lewis.

I say that NRLE is a front for the MPP because MPP went to great lengths to keep its role a secret as long as possible. It is not a secret now.

There is an Internet mailing list (ARO) for the leaders of " reform organizations. " I am not on the list, but I have numerous friends who are, and I regularly receive copies of exchanges relevant to cannabis. MPP is on the list, of course.

MPP CEO Rob Kampia has been waging a war on NORML since I fired him. Actually, before.
For some background see

And now he is claiming on the ARO list that " NORML has turned out to be our primary opponent in the Nevada campaign; even the drug czar's rhetoric has been more helpful, as evidenced by the July 25 article in the Las Vegas Review-Journal, whose headline read Marijuana law change would not prompt federal crackdown. "! "

Of course, we know that John Walters would never lie, but what did he really say?
See

According to the July 25th article in the Las Vegas Review-Journal, Walters said, " If Nevadans vote to legalize the possession of 3 ounces or less of marijuana, the federal government will not " strong arm " them by stepping up the enforcement of federal drug possession laws "

Actually, believe it or not, Walters is almost certainly telling the truth here, but read the red print. He is talking about possession, because the Feds simply do not have the resources to arrest users, and Stroup was talking about the part of the initiative under which the NRLE web site says " adults could obtain marijuana through a legally regulated market. "

In other words, Walters was talking about possession and Stroup was talking about sales, and Kampia is misrepresenting both.

This weekend it got even more bizarre.

Billy Rogers, Kampia's man at NRLE, was on CNN's Crossfire, which is a parody of political debate on which Robert Novak presents a parody of " conservatism. "

Here is the relevant exchange:

" NOVAK: Mr. Rogers, I would like to quote for you somebody -- I'm not a big hard-line anti-drug person -- I'd like to quote for you Keith Stroup who is with the National Organization for the Reform of Marijuana Laws, NORML.

And Keith Stroup says this, quote: It is highly unlikely the federal government would allow a state to create a legal market for the sale of drugs, in which the state licenses the sale or sets up stores to sell it, end quote.

Are you just making money for yourself, but the feds ain't going to allow it, are they?

BILLY ROGERS, NEVADANS FOR RESPONSIBLE LAW ENFORCEMENT: Well, Keith Stroup should have talked to the drug czar, because when the drug czar was out there two weeks ago, he said that the federal government would not crack down on Nevadans if this initiative passes in November.

I mean, the federal government is not going to come in here and arrest people for small amounts of marijuana. That's simply not going to happen.

And when the drug czar came to town, perhaps Keith Stroup didn't read that.

NOVAK: Well, I don't know -- which drug czar are you talking about?

ROGERS: I'm talking about John Walters.

NOVAK: John Walters is really against this. He thinks it's a disgrace.

This is really classic bait and switch. Novak, a prohibitionist, or at least he plays one on television, accurately quotes Keith Stroup in the context of allowing sales, but for some reason Rogers thinks that pretending that the Feds will permit sales of cannabis for recreational use -- while they are busy shutting down clubs in California that sell to medical users -- will somehow convince Nevadans to vote for the initiative. So he says that " perhaps Keith Stroup didn't read that. "
See

In fact, the best response the honest response -- would have been simply to say that this is a challenge to the Feds, and that Nevada should be ready for the Feds to back off on marijuana prohibition. Many Nevadans would respond favorably to a challenge to the Feds.

But how does Kampia react to this?

He sent out the following:

" Unfortunately, the fall-out from Keith's harmful rhetoric continues. Last night on CNN's " Crossfire ", the first barb that was thrown at Billy Rogers was a quote from Keith that the bad guys (Bob Novak) are now using against us. After the drug czar visited Las Vegas on July 25 and provided us with his favorable perspective on the role of the federal government, we were in good shape. But now, since Keith's unhelpful quotes in The New York Times one week ago, we are in the position of having to debate against Keith's perspective, and we're using the drug czar's position in our defense. "

Now there are going to be those who say that I should not be hanging the reform movement's dirty laundry out to dry. We should all be united and just ignore the fact that the best funded reform organization is being led by a person who lies about what others in the movement are saying because he can't control the spin.

And the person who is leading the Nevada initiative is misrepresenting both NORML's position and the Drug Czar's while claiming that the head of NORML does not know what Walters said.

This is not something that should be kept private.

Now let's look at the choice of Nevada in the first place.

Nevada is unique in that an initiative that amends the state constitution has to be approved by the voters TWICE. If Question 9 passes this November, nothing will change. It will require a second vote in two years.

Had the initiative effort been waged in Oregon, I think that it would have had at least as good a chance of passing, and it would not require a second campaign. If it failed the first time, we could go back in two years, and try again.

And Oregon has some excellent activists. But then that might be a problem. They might have wanted to have some say in what was going to be done about cannabis policies in their state, and worse, they might want a little credit if it passes.

And there is another problem on the horizon for this fall in Nevada.

There is a second round of an initiative to bar gay marriages that is strongly backed by the Mormon church, which will spend huge sums to get out its voters. (Nevada has a large Mormon population.) That issue is certain to bring out the social conservative vote generally and these voters are unlikely to support an initiative to legalize marijuana.

Ironically, these same conservative voters might respond favorably to a challenge to the Federal government based on state's rights! But they won't hear any such argument from NRLE, because it wants to pretend that the Feds won't do anything.

How did this happen? Well, I really don't know.

MPP declined to share its polling data or to include others in its decision to make Nevada the target, or in the choice of language in the initiative. It made all the decisions and then decided that everyone else had the obligation to lie about what the initiative really says.

Consequently, I am not particularly optimistic about Question 9. I hope it passes, but if it does not, it will not be a great loss for the movement. However, the reform movement will be very much the loser if we do not demand ethical leadership.

When I first said that " Freedom has nothing to fear from the truth, " I was not just talking about the lying by the prohibitionists, but also those supposedly on our side who were afraid that telling the truth might hurt us.

All we have is the truth.
